title: The One With Rosss Wedding

jokes.text: Six-hour trip to London. That's a lot of Monica.
jokes.setup: Monica is frantically rushing everyone out the door, checking things obsessively.
jokes.punchline: Chandler reduces the terror of the trip not to jet lag or customs, but to the sheer volume of Monica-ness they'll have to endure.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical. The joke reframes a six-hour flight not as a geographic journey but as an endurance test of Monica's personality. It's specific, character-driven, and lands with the audience before the credits roll. Only Chandler could deliver this, and it sets the comedic tone of the episode immediately. Near 8+ territory due to character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We need to leave in four hours! Everyone pack now!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, relax. That's plenty of time.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No it's not! The plane leaves early!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Early? Monica, planes don't leave early.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This one does! It's a very ambitious plane. It has dreams!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, is it a time-traveling plane?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yes! Exactly! It's already left!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, we're standing in the apartment.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Which means we're already late for a plane that left tomorrow!

jokes.text: Monica explaining the 'check' system to herself, admitting her mom does it, then Chandler reveals his mom used to put her head in the oven — 'Actually, she only did it the one time. But it was pretty weird.'
jokes.setup: Monica's charming-but-odd habit of saying 'check' out loud to herself, defending it as something her mom taught her.
jokes.punchline: Chandler casually one-ups with a suicide attempt anecdote, then walks it back with devastating understatement: 'only the one time... but it was pretty weird.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is exquisite: Monica sets up a mundane 'my mom does it' defense, and Chandler weaponizes the same 'my mom' format with something catastrophically darker. The understatement 'it was pretty weird' after implying a suicide attempt is what elevates this from shocking to genuinely funny. It's deeply Chandler — his deflection of pain through dark humor is core to his character. High originality because it subverts the cozy mom-habits conversation so completely.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So... that was the in-flight entertainment?

jokes.text: Ross asks if Joey has his passport. Joey: 'Yeah, in my third drawer of my dresser. You don't wanna lose that.'
jokes.setup: Ross checks if Joey has his passport, expecting a normal travel-ready answer.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he left his passport at home — in his dresser — and delivers the line about not wanting to lose it with cheerful, clueless confidence.
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey stupidity joke, but elevated by the specific detail ('third drawer') and the deadpan wisdom tag about not losing it. The irony is entirely lost on him, which is perfect. Character integration score is high because only Joey could be this helpfully clueless.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, are those condoms?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Don't read my condoms!

jokes.text: 'London, baby!' / 'Because that's not gonna get annoying.' / 'London, baby!'
jokes.setup: Joey enthusiastically yells 'London, baby!' as they depart.
jokes.punchline: Chandler sarcastically predicts it'll get annoying; Joey immediately proves him right.
jokes.explanation: The setup and instant payoff is well-structured. 'London, baby!' becomes a running gag seed. Chandler's meta-prediction and its immediate confirmation is the kind of tight construction that makes the show feel well-written. Gets rewatch bonus because the gag will recur.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Passport? Check. Tickets? Check. Hotel confirmation? Check. Traveler's checks? Check.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I love saying check to myself. Check!

jokes.text: Phoebe, very pregnant and unable to get up, asks Ross for a hug but also asks him to bring her the newspaper.
jokes.setup: Phoebe warmly says she wants to give Ross a hug before he leaves but can't get up.
jokes.punchline: She asks Ross to come to her — and then casually tacks on 'can you bring me the newspaper?' treating her immobility as a convenience.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's pregnancy becomes a vehicle for gentle selfishness. The joke works because the emotional warmth of the hug request makes the newspaper ask land as a funny pivot. Phoebe-specific character humor.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, mom does it!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, and mom also puts her head in the oven.

jokes.text: Chandler goes in to hug Phoebe, and she asks him to bring her book from the counter in his apartment.
jokes.setup: Pattern established with Ross: hug + bonus errand request.
jokes.punchline: The book is in Chandler's apartment, escalating the inconvenience of the errand.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the previous joke — the book being in a different apartment ups the ante. The running gag is well-deployed here, though it's not as fresh as the first beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It was only once!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Still pretty weird though.

jokes.text: Joey tells Chandler to 'do something' repeatedly; Chandler: 'I am. I'm ignoring you.'
jokes.setup: Joey is bored or restless and badgering Chandler to entertain him.
jokes.punchline: Chandler reframes his inaction as a deliberate activity: ignoring Joey.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler deadpan. Very economical — the joke is entirely in the reframing of a passive state as an active choice. The character integration is strong because Chandler's brand of passive-aggressive wit is his defining trait.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Where's your passport? We need to leave for the airport soon.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, it's in my dresser drawer at home.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Your dresser drawer? Ross, we're leaving now!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, I know. I'll just... I'll go get it.

jokes.text: Emily rattles off a cascade of wedding disasters: wrong chicken, no tulips, cellist has carpal tunnel.
jokes.setup: Ross asks what's wrong. Emily begins listing wedding catastrophes.
jokes.punchline: The list keeps escalating from food substitution to medical condition affecting the musician — each item more absurd than the last.
jokes.explanation: Classic wedding-chaos escalation list. The carpal tunnel detail is the funniest item — specific and medical in a way that's incongruous with wedding planning. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: London, baby!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's not going to get annoying at all.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: London, baby!

jokes.text: Joey filming at Westminster Abbey asks Chandler what he thinks; Chandler says they're thinking of changing the name — 'To Put the Camera Away.'
jokes.setup: Joey is enthusiastically filming everything tourist-style at Westminster Abbey and asks Chandler for his thoughts.
jokes.punchline: Chandler invents a fake name-change for the Abbey as a passive-aggressive way to tell Joey to stop filming.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most polished jokes. The setup (Joey asking an earnest tourist question) is perfectly baited. Chandler's response — presenting an absurd fictional fact with complete deadpan sincerity — is both a great joke and a perfect expression of his character's irritated wit. The structure is immaculate: the misdirection of 'they're thinking of changing the name' makes the punchline land harder. Approaches the 8-anchor territory.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I want to hug you goodbye but I can't get up.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, okay, I'll help you up.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: While you're up, could you bring me the newspaper?

jokes.text: 'They're thinking of changing the name.' 'Really? To what?' 'To Put the Camera Away.'
jokes.setup: Joey is enthusiastically filming everything and asks Chandler what he thinks of the abbey.
jokes.punchline: Chandler invents a fake abbey renaming as a passive-aggressive way to tell Joey to stop filming him.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is perfect: Chandler plays along with Joey's interview framing long enough to bait him into 'Really? To what?' then deploys the punchline. It's a layered joke — it works as a complaint, as a bit of deadpan absurdism, and as a character moment. Highly quotable. The misdirection (you expect a real answer) is flawlessly executed.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Chandler, could you bring a book from your apartment?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why? What book?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Any book. I just want to see if you actually own one.

jokes.text: Joey's comeback: 'Man, you are Westminster Crabby.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has just been passive-aggressively dismissive.
jokes.punchline: Joey riffs on 'Westminster' to coin 'Westminster Crabby' — a genuinely Joey-esque portmanteau putdown.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the specific word construction — 'Westminster Crabby' is funny because it's simultaneously stupid and clever. Joey inventing a location-pun insult is completely in character; it's the kind of wordplay that only works in his mouth. High quotability because it's the sort of line audiences repeat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Goodbye, Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Goodbye, Pheebs.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Goodbye, Phoeb-o.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Goodbye, Phobby.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Goodbye, Phoeb-a-dob.

jokes.text: Phoebe's wedgie confession: 'Okay, I have a wedgie.' Chandler: 'Okay, that is all you.'
jokes.setup: Chandler is doting on the very pregnant Phoebe, asking what she needs.
jokes.punchline: She asks him to fix her wedgie; he immediately draws a firm line.
jokes.explanation: Quick, efficient comedic beat. The oversharing is the joke, and Chandler's refusal is the punchline. 'That is all you' is a quotable line. Not groundbreaking but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How you doin'?

jokes.text: Okay, that is all you.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just told Chandler she has a wedgie and needs help with it.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's instant, flat refusal — 'that is all you' — treats the request as categorically off-limits without any drama.
jokes.explanation: The button to the wedgie joke. Tight, in character, perfectly economical. Functions as the second beat of a two-beat joke — both are needed to get the full laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, they left me! They all left me! Oh... well, I don't need them. I don't need anything from anybody. I'm fine on my own.

jokes.text: Phoebe accidentally reveals Rachel is 'still in love with Ross' — a secret apparently everyone knows.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is sympathizing with Rachel about the awkwardness of going to Ross's wedding, saying 'If someone I was still in love with was...'
jokes.punchline: She lets slip 'still in love with' and can't walk it back — the secret everyone knows comes tumbling out.
jokes.explanation: The accidental revelation is a classic sitcom engine, but executed with reasonable craft here. The comedy is in Phoebe's immediate backpedal attempt and the dawning horror on Rachel's face. Rewatch bonus because this scene triggers the season's major plot point.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, you have to do something about this!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I am doing something. I'm ignoring it.

jokes.text: If someone I was still in love with was— / Still in love with? / Yeah. / I'm not in love with Ross.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying to comfort Rachel about how she left things with Ross, starting a sentence about understanding why Rachel didn't go.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe accidentally reveals she (and apparently everyone) knows Rachel is still in love with Ross — a secret Rachel didn't know she was keeping, or at least not admitting.
jokes.explanation: This is the structural linchpin of the Rachel/Ross storyline in this episode, and it's executed with great craft. The accidental slip ('still in love with') followed by Rachel's immediate denial sets off a brilliantly written escalating self-revelation sequence. High impact because it's a cringe-comedy moment that also advances the story significantly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. If I'm here on the map, and the map is here... doesn't that mean I'm trapped inside the map?

jokes.text: Rachel's self-deceiving spiral: 'clearly I have feelings... loving feelings... continuing feelings of love... sexual feelings... but I do love him.'
jokes.setup: Rachel insists she is NOT in love with Ross, then tries to qualify her feelings into non-love.
jokes.punchline: Each qualification digs her deeper until she's listed every possible component of love while insisting she's not in love.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully structured escalation joke. Each sentence contradicts the previous denial while Rachel's confidence remains intact. The structure is the joke — it's essentially a comedic syllogism that arrives at the exact opposite of its premise. Strong character integration because Rachel's self-deception is a core character trait. The rhythm of the escalation is well-written.

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: If you can't behave, you're going to get a time out.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A time out? What are you, my mother?

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: It's a British thing!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, in America, we call it being sent to your room like a child.

jokes.text: Phoebe: 'We thought you knew.' Rachel: 'We?' Phoebe: 'Yeah, we all know. We talk about it all the time.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is shocked Phoebe knew she was in love with Ross.
jokes.punchline: Not only does Phoebe know, but all their friends know, and they actively discuss it — Rachel is the only one oblivious.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying comedic beat that uses dramatic irony well. The reveal that the whole friend group gossips about Rachel's feelings while she's oblivious is funny and character-revealing. 'We talk about it all the time' is the stronger of the two beats.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, chicken has salmonella, so salmon must have... chicknella.

jokes.text: Phoebe comparing telling Rachel about her feelings to telling Monica 'Hey, you like things clean.'
jokes.setup: Rachel asks why no one told her about her obvious feelings for Ross.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe analogizes it to stating the most obvious possible fact about Monica — 'you like things clean' — implying Rachel's feelings are equally self-evident.
jokes.explanation: Elegant double-character joke — it simultaneously characterizes Rachel's obliviousness and Monica's cleanliness obsession in a single analogy. The understatement ('you like things clean') as a descriptor for Monica is itself funny. Phoebe-specific delivery that works well.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The building's being demolished.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Apparently it was scheduled. They told us three months ago.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We were planning a wedding!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, the building was planning to not exist.

jokes.text: Joey at a London market, seeing the novelty 'I'm with stupid' hat: 'Well, I'm not gonna have to buy that I'm With Stupid T-shirt anymore.'
jokes.setup: Joey is excited about a novelty tourist hat (implied to be an absurd hat with an arrow or similar joke item).
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he already owns (or intended to buy) an 'I'm with stupid' shirt — confirming that he already self-applies this label to their friendship dynamic.
jokes.explanation: Decent joke that reveals Joey is comfortable being the 'stupid' one in the duo, which is character-consistent. The punchline relies on the audience catching the implication quickly. Not particularly original but well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's nice and all, but I've seen better abbeys.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'How can I answer that when I'm pretending I don't know you?'
jokes.setup: Joey asks Chandler if he embarrasses him, while Chandler has physically distanced himself from the hat-wearing Joey.
jokes.punchline: Chandler reveals he's already in full stranger-mode, making the question moot.
jokes.explanation: Very economical and well-structured. The humor is in the revelation that Chandler has already performed a social retreat before even being asked. The logic is airtight and the delivery would be perfect for a deadpan actor. High economy score.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So what do you think of the Abbey?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's great, Joey. You know what would make it even better? If you stopped filming everything and actually experienced life for once.

jokes.text: Street vendor: 'They're all tourists.' (explaining why no Londoners are wearing the novelty hats)
jokes.setup: Joey points out that no actual Londoners are wearing the novelty hats the vendor claims all Londoners wear.
jokes.punchline: The vendor dismisses every visible person as a tourist — an unfalsifiable and self-serving defense.
jokes.explanation: Three-word punchline that is logically absurd and funny. The character integration is low because this is a walk-on vendor, but the joke itself is tightly constructed. The circular, unfalsifiable reasoning is the comedic engine.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What's with Chandler? He's being so crabby.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's upset about Westminster Abbey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Westminster? More like West-Crab-ster!

jokes.text: Joey, given the choice between Chandler's companionship and the hat, chooses the hat without hesitation.
jokes.setup: Chandler ultimatums Joey — the hat or me.
jokes.punchline: Joey doesn't hesitate. The hat wins.
jokes.explanation: Joey's child-like attachment to things — food, hats, comfort — over relationships is perfect character comedy. The lack of hesitation is the punch. Works well in the context of the running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I'm probably going to spill something on this dress before the wedding even starts.

jokes.text: Ross losing his temper about postponing the wedding, referring to Monica's 'teeny, tiny little brain'
jokes.setup: Ross is furious that Monica suggested postponing the wedding to Emily.
jokes.punchline: His rant escalates to insulting Monica in absurdly escalating terms: 'teeny, tiny little brain.'
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny in context — Ross's self-righteous spiral is a known character trait. The 'teeny, tiny little brain' phrase is cartoonish rather than sharp. Gets by on Ross's escalating ridiculousness.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So your wedding is just... Sunday with a spectacular amount of food?

dialogue.speaker: Emily
dialogue.line: Well, when you put it that way, it doesn't sound so bad.

jokes.text: Huh? Do you think my sister's teeny, tiny little brain comprehends that people took time out of their lives to fly thousands of miles to be here?
jokes.setup: Ross has just found out Monica suggested postponing the wedding, and he's furious — apparently unaware Monica is right behind him.
jokes.punchline: Ross delivers a withering attack on Monica's intelligence while she is presumably present or about to be revealed as present. The 'teeny, tiny little brain' escalation is both funny and revealing of Ross at his worst.
jokes.explanation: This is funny primarily because of the dramatic irony — the audience knows or suspects Monica is nearby, so his tirade is both funny and cringe-inducing. 'Teeny, tiny little brain' is a bit broad, but the anger-blindness is Ross-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, there is one thing. Could you be my surrogate?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No!

jokes.text: 'Don't you point your pants at me.'
jokes.setup: Ross is gesturing angrily at Emily during their argument.
jokes.punchline: Emily's command to stop 'pointing his pants' at her is surreally specific and funny — apparently he's directing his trouser-clad gesture threateningly.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. 'Don't you point your pants at me' is an absurdist construction that is immediately understood (he's pointing aggressively while arguing) but worded in the most unexpected way possible. It undercuts a tense dramatic argument with a phrase that makes no literal sense but perfect emotional sense. High quotability — this line has genuine cultural staying power. The economy is near-perfect: five words that defuse tension and generate a laugh simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my god, Rachel, you're so in love with him!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?! No, I'm not! Phoebe, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Come on, it's so obvious. You light up whenever he walks in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That is crazy. I do not light up. And I am certainly not in love with anyone.

jokes.text: Ross: 'What are you saying, it's now or never?' Emily: 'No, I'm saying it's now.' Ross: 'Or?' Emily: 'There's no or in mine.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Emily are in a tense argument about whether to postpone the wedding.
jokes.punchline: Their semantic breakdown over the phrase 'now or never' — Emily insisting hers has no 'or' — creates an absurd logic game inside a dramatic fight.
jokes.explanation: A clever bit of wordplay embedded in genuine dramatic tension. The comedy comes from Emily's pedantic insistence on the literal grammar of a phrase Ross uses. 'There's no or in mine' is a great line — precise, funny, and character-revealing (Emily is clearly someone who means what she says exactly). Well-structured exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, he's smart, he's funny, he's sweet... and he's always there when I need him.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Plus, he gets me. He really gets me.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And when he looks at me, I feel like... like I'm the only person in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, I love him. I love Ross!

jokes.text: Immediately after the 'or' debate, Ross says: 'What is wrong with these pants?'
jokes.setup: Emily has just told Ross 'it's not the pants, it's you who's backwards' — a metaphorical statement about their relationship.
jokes.punchline: Ross takes the pants comment completely literally in the middle of an existential argument.
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-timed absurdist beat. Ross's oblivious literal interpretation of a metaphor while his fiancée has essentially just threatened to call off the wedding is funny because of the tonal collision. His character's tendency toward missing the emotional point is well-used here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh come on, it's so obvious! It's like saying the sky is blue, water is wet, and Joey's gay.

jokes.text: Rachel on her failed shopping therapy: 'Manhattan does not have enough stores.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks if shopping helped Rachel feel better about Ross.
jokes.punchline: Rachel implies she tried to shop away her feelings but exhausted the retail capacity of all of Manhattan.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character joke — Rachel's coping mechanism being shopping, taken to its logical extreme. The line is economical, quotable, and deeply Rachel. 'Manhattan does not have enough stores' as an expression of emotional devastation is funny in its hyperbolic specificity. High character integration because this is a uniquely Rachel statement.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, what do you mean Joey? Joey doesn't clean!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, I meant Monica. Monica's the one who's always cleaning.

jokes.text: Phoebe's spell ingredients: photos of Ross, chocolate, tepid water — Rachel asks if it involves graveyard dirt hanging from a north-facing tree; Phoebe says 'Only if you have the hiccups too.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe offers to help Rachel get over Ross using a photo, chocolate, and tepid water — a seemingly magical/ritual setup.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's escalating guess about graveyard dirt earns Phoebe confirming it, but only as a hiccup cure — a surreal condition that reveals Phoebe's magical system has its own internal logic.
jokes.explanation: A great Phoebe joke because it commits fully to her magical worldview while adding an unexpected layer of internal logic. The graveyard dirt ritual having a secondary application — specifically for hiccups — implies Phoebe has a whole taxonomy of spiritual remedies. The specificity ('north-facing tree') is what elevates it from generically weird to sharply written.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Joey! Where did you get that hat?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I like it! It's cool!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, it really says 'I have no idea what I'm doing.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No it doesn't!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey, it's a hat that screams 'I'm an idiot.' You don't even have to open your mouth.

jokes.text: Phoebe's spell reveal: the picture is for Rachel, but the chocolate and water are for Phoebe — she just didn't feel like getting up.
jokes.setup: Phoebe presents a ritual with three components (photo, chocolate, water) as a treatment for Rachel's feelings.
jokes.punchline: Two of the three components are purely for Phoebe's own comfort. She used Rachel's vulnerability to get snacks.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed misdirection. The audience is led to believe Phoebe has a genuine (if eccentric) healing ritual. The reveal that it was a snack delivery scheme is both a betrayal of expectations and completely in character — Phoebe being pregnant and unable to move makes the lazy selfishness even funnier. The structure is excellent: the setup is long enough to fully commit the audience to the bit before the rug pull.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why won't you just respond?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Because I'm disowning you. Publicly. I'm going to the town square, I'm going to ring the bell, and I'm going to shout, 'This man is not my friend!'

jokes.text: Before we get started, I just wanna say, for the record, I love Ross. I think he's such a great guy.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is about to begin aversion therapy to make Rachel stop loving Ross — the whole point is to break the attachment.
jokes.punchline: Before the anti-Ross therapy begins, Rachel provides an on-the-record pro-Ross statement — completely undermining the stated goal of the therapy before it starts.
jokes.explanation: The 'for the record' framing and the timing (right before anti-Ross therapy) is excellent. It's a subtle joke about how deep Rachel's self-sabotage goes. Good character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: If you wear that hat, I'm leaving.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay.

jokes.text: Phoebe's aversion therapy: 'imagine you're running your hands through his hair... but, oh, ew, gross, it's some kind of grease...' Rachel: 'his hair was always more crunchy than greasy.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is trying aversion therapy — guiding Rachel through an imagined encounter with Ross, then introducing a repulsive detail about his hair.
jokes.punchline: Rachel corrects Phoebe's hair description from 'greasy' to 'crunchy' — revealing she has precise, firsthand knowledge of Ross's hair texture, which only deepens how in love she still is.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke because the punchline reveals what it's supposed to cure — Rachel's intimate knowledge of Ross's hair proves she's still very much in love. 'Crunchy' as a hair texture descriptor is both specific and gross in a funny way. The therapy failing is funnier than if it had worked.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, how you doin'? I'm Joey Tribbiani. I'm an actor.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So, uh, where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: British Woman
dialogue.line: London.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, England! Yeah, I love England. Fish and chips, the Queen, soccer... I mean, football.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm basically representing my entire country right now, and I'm nailing it.

jokes.text: Phoebe pinches Rachel as aversion therapy; Rachel: 'Well, I like you less.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe pivots to physical aversion therapy — pinching Rachel while she looks at Ross's photo.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's summary response is not 'I feel less attracted to Ross' but 'I like you less' — the therapy only created an aversion to Phoebe.
jokes.explanation: Four-word punchline that's nearly perfect in economy. 'I like you less' captures the exact wrong outcome of aversion therapy with beautiful compression. The structure is tight: build the expectation of the therapy working, deliver the entirely misdirected result. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Postpone the wedding? Monica, I don't think you understand the situation here. You have a teeny, tiny, little brain.

jokes.text: Okay. How do you feel now? / Well, I like you less.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just physically hurt Rachel as part of her aversion therapy and asks how she feels.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's response indicates the therapy transferred the aversion from Ross to Phoebe, not from Rachel to Ross — a completely logical and funny misfire.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical punchline. 'I like you less' is exactly the right response — it's what aversion therapy literally produced, just directed at the therapist. The logic is tight, the delivery flat, and it's highly quotable. One of the better one-liners in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Don't point at me! I'm wearing sweatpants!

jokes.text: Chandler's apology: 'I shouldn't have said you were embarrassing me. That really wasn't cool. And if it makes you feel any better, I've had a really lousy day.' Joey: 'Me too.' / 'No! I had the best day ever.'
jokes.setup: Chandler sincerely apologizes and says he's had a lousy day, expecting sympathy.
jokes.punchline: Joey initially agrees he's had a bad day — then immediately reverses to announce it was 'the best day ever,' revealing he was just saying what Chandler wanted to hear.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure. Joey's 'Me too' is a beat of sweet fake solidarity followed by an instant, gleeful contradiction. 'No! I had the best day ever.' delivers on two levels: it's funny as a reversal, and it confirms Joey's day (meeting Fergie, etc.) while also showing Joey doesn't really understand how to do emotional support. The exclamation, the reversal, and the character truth make this one of the episode's best comedy beats.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Did shopping help you feel better?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Phoebe, I went to like five stores today and I couldn't find a single thing I wanted to buy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: That's terrible.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know! It's like, what is the point of living in Manhattan if you can't find anything to spend money on?

jokes.text: Joey has met Fergie — the Duchess of York — by getting lost in his map.
jokes.setup: Joey brags about his best day ever; Chandler doesn't know what's coming.
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals he met Fergie — and the reason is as absurd as possible: he got lost in his giant tourist map and stumbled into her.
jokes.explanation: A callback payoff that earns its impact. The earlier map joke (at 04:33) established Joey's hopelessly lost state, and now we learn that absurd incompetence led to a celebrity encounter. The juxtaposition of incompetence and reward is very Joey. The callback structure gives it additional craft points.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Does your ritual involve graveyard dirt and trees?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, yeah. Unless she has hiccups. Then I'd need a virgin and a sack of goats.

jokes.text: Fergie tells Chandler she thinks Joey's hat is 'kind of dashing.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has been humiliated all day by Joey's tacky tourist hat.
jokes.punchline: The Duchess of York — British royalty — endorses the hat, retroactively vindicating Joey and maximally embarrassing Chandler's taste.
jokes.explanation: The hat running gag gets a perfect payoff. Having a member of the British royal family validate the tackiest tourist item Chandler has been mocking all day is a great comedic reversal. The specificity of it being Fergie — and 'dashing' as her word choice — adds flavor.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, I need you to do exactly what I say. First, take this chocolate and dissolve it in warm water.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, what is this for?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's a very ancient and sacred ritual. You cannot question it.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Now drink it slowly and think pure thoughts.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, why are we really doing this?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because I'm hungry and I didn't want to just ask for snacks.

jokes.text: Monica tells Ross and Emily she talked to Emily and 'you are welcome.' Ross: 'Am I?' — the reversal reveal that Monica's advice backfired.
jokes.setup: Monica confidently announces she helped by talking to Emily and expects gratitude.
jokes.punchline: Ross's flat 'Am I?' signals that Monica's well-intentioned advice caused Emily to nearly call off the wedding.
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Monica's confidence in one word ('Am I?') is economically excellent. The structure relies on the audience's dawning realization that Monica's fix made things worse, which is classic sitcom irony. Character-integrated — Monica's controlling helpfulness backfiring is very on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, Rachel, maybe you should think about Ross's flaws more. Like his hair.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: His hair? What's wrong with his hair? It's so... voluminous. And the way it just kind of poofs out at the sides, especially when it's humid. And sometimes he uses too much product so it gets all greasy and stringy, and it sticks to his forehead. Plus he never gets it trimmed properly so it's always kind of an awkward length, not quite long enough to pull back but too long to look neat, and the color is so... mousy.

jokes.text: Monica: 'Oh, my God. You're even dumber than I am.'
jokes.setup: Ross explains that he told Emily it was stupid to put off the wedding just because the hall was gone.
jokes.punchline: Monica, who gave Emily the idea to postpone, realizes Ross has made things worse and judges herself harshly relative to him — a funny self-deprecating reversal.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that works because Monica's self-awareness (even when calling herself dumb) is funnier than a generic insult. The 'dumber than I am' construction implies Monica already considers herself pretty dumb in this situation, which is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, that hurt.

jokes.text: Monica explaining the wedding-planning fantasy: 'Ever since the first time she took a pillowcase and hung it off her head... That's what we did.'
jokes.setup: Monica is explaining to Ross why Emily needs the perfect venue — it's been a lifelong dream.
jokes.punchline: Monica reveals she and presumably all little girls did the pillowcase veil trick, fully committing to the detail as universal female experience.
jokes.explanation: A warm observational joke about childhood wedding fantasies. The specificity of the pillowcase detail is what makes it land — it's precise enough to feel true. Monica's earnestness and self-inclusion ('That's what we did') is well-played.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I had a lousy day.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, me too.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, no! I had an audition and I got the part!

jokes.text: Monica's wedding fantasy includes: 'the perfect four-tiered wedding cake [strained voice] with the little people on top.'
jokes.setup: Monica is passionately describing the perfect wedding dream — perfect place, perfect guy.
jokes.punchline: The 'four-tiered wedding cake with the little people on top' delivered in a strained, emotionally overwrought voice reveals this is Monica's specific fantasy being described, not just Emily's. Monica is basically confessing her own wedding obsession.
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the tell — Monica's voice straining with barely suppressed longing reveals she's describing her own fantasy, not empathizing with Emily's. The 'four-tiered' specificity and 'little people on top' are Monica details. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God! You're not gonna believe who I just saw at the hotel!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not even kidding, it was... How you doin'?

jokes.text: Ross: 'That pillowcase thing, I thought you guys were just doing The Flying Nun.' Monica: 'Sometimes we were.'
jokes.setup: Monica has just finished an emotional speech about childhood wedding fantasies involving pillowcase veils.
jokes.punchline: Ross completely misread the activity — he thought it was a Flying Nun impression. Monica's 'Sometimes we were' admits the dual use, puncturing the romanticism.
jokes.explanation: A smart joke that undercuts Monica's romantic monologue perfectly. Ross's obliviousness is both funny and in character. But Monica's 'sometimes we were' is the real punchline — by admitting it, she both validates the joke AND maintains a trace of the fantasy (they were doing BOTH things). The dual-meaning admission is clever writing.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You told her you'd postpone the wedding? Ross, that's not postponing, that's canceling!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know what I said, okay? I panicked!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, at least you're consistent. You panic, you say stupid things... it's like you're a human version of me before coffee.

jokes.text: I had no idea. That pillowcase thing, I thought you guys were just doing The Flying Nun.
jokes.setup: Monica has just delivered a heartfelt speech about the significance of a little girl's wedding fantasies, clearly moving Ross.
jokes.punchline: Ross completely misread the pillowcase-veil ritual his entire childhood — he thought the girls were playing 'The Flying Nun' (a 1960s TV show), not rehearsing their weddings.
jokes.explanation: A great callback punchline. The Flying Nun is the perfect alternative interpretation — it's era-appropriate and equally plausible visually. Ross's misreading of a universal childhood ritual for his entire life reveals his obliviousness in a funny, specific way.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know, ever since we were little, girls dream about their wedding day. We think about the dress, the flowers, the cake... and the little people on top.

jokes.text: I hope Ross didn't think we went in there because we were uncomfortable out here. / I hope he did.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica ducked into a bathroom or separate space during Ross and Emily's argument; they reemerge.
jokes.punchline: Chandler worries about optics; Monica reveals she actively WANTED Ross to think they fled from discomfort — the rare confession of pure social cowardice.
jokes.explanation: Monica's flat 'I hope he did' is a great reversal — it admits to something most people would deny, and the admission is funnier than any attempt to justify it would have been. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, you were playing Flying Nun?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, sometimes.

jokes.text: Phoebe calls to Joey: 'I just saw someone that looks just like you on the subway. I was gonna go over and say hi, but then I figured he doesn't care he looks like you.'
jokes.setup: Phoebe answers the phone excited to tell Joey something.
jokes.punchline: The story has no payoff for Joey — Phoebe decided not to approach his lookalike because that person doesn't care he resembles Joey. The logic is impeccable in a completely Phoebe way.
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully Phoebe-specific piece of logic. The joke is that she started a story with apparent purpose and arrived at a conclusion that's both nihilistic and perfectly reasoned from her perspective. 'He doesn't care he looks like you' is the kind of observation only Phoebe would make, and only Phoebe would consider it a complete story worth sharing. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that guy totally looks like Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Really? Where?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Over there. But don't look, he'll know we're talking about him.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Phoebe, why would he care if he looks like me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I don't know, some people are sensitive about these things. I once knew a guy who looked like Coolio, and he got really upset when people pointed it out.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But Coolio probably cares. I'm awesome!

jokes.text: Joey: 'That just cost me 4 bucks.' (realizing Phoebe called him from across the ocean just to tell him that)
jokes.setup: Phoebe has just delivered a pointless international phone call story.
jokes.punchline: Joey's only concern is the transatlantic call cost — '$4' — a perfectly mundane response to Phoebe's bizarre non-story.
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfectly placed. Joey's reaction grounds the absurdity in mundane economics, which is the right comedic choice. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Seven people miss me.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Aww, that's sweet. Although, I'm not sure if those are babies missing you or if I'm just hungry.

jokes.text: Joey: 'All right, well, the seven of us miss you.' Rachel: 'Who's seven?' Joey lists: 'me, Rachel, the birds, the babies.'
jokes.setup: Joey says 'the seven of us miss you' — an odd number given the known cast present in New York.
jokes.punchline: His count includes himself, Rachel, two birds, and apparently multiple babies — the math doesn't quite work but Joey is entirely confident.
jokes.explanation: Joey's math is the joke — he includes animals and unborn babies in his count with casual confidence. 'The babies miss me?' from Phoebe is a sweet, funny response. The joke gently plays with Joey's inclusive, childlike worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. Two pizzas?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, one pepperoni, one cheese.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But I only ordered one pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, but I added another one because I thought you'd want extra.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You what?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Where is it?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It's on its way!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no, cancel it!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I can't cancel it!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Because I don't know where it is!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Then find out where it is!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I don't know! It's just... out there somewhere!

jokes.text: Joey ordered the 'Joey Special' — two pizzas — without Joey, explaining 'we were thinking about you.'
jokes.setup: Joey is told they ordered pizza without him, and they ordered the 'Joey Special.'
jokes.punchline: The Joey Special is two pizzas — a standing order so ingrained it has a name. The irony of ordering Joey's signature order 'in his memory' while eating it themselves is funny.
jokes.explanation: A great character joke — the fact that Joey's pizza order has a formal name is the first funny layer. The second is the rationalization that eating his special while he's away is a tribute. The third is Joey's most urgent question: where did they order from. Priorities perfectly intact.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: If it rains at the outdoor wedding, we'll get wet.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, at least you'll have a date to get wet with. I'll be getting wet alone.

jokes.text: Joey, upon learning they ordered the Joey Special in his absence, doesn't express outrage at being excluded — he asks 'Where did you get it from?' before the line goes dead.
jokes.setup: Joey is processing being excluded from a pizza order made in his honor.
jokes.punchline: His priority is not emotional — it's logistical. He needs to know the pizzeria.
jokes.explanation: Joey's character is crystallized in this moment — his values are fully food-centric. The line going dead before he gets his answer is a good comedic button. Character integration is very high.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I just want Ross to have all the information.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, please! You just want to break him and Emily up so you can have him for yourself. You're just jealous of that British chippy!

jokes.text: Cheers theme song plays on TV while Phoebe and Rachel sit in sadness — visual/audio comedic juxtaposition.
jokes.setup: Rachel is emotionally devastated, Phoebe is trying to help; they sit in silence.
jokes.punchline: The 'Cheers' theme ('Where Everybody Knows Your Name') plays on the TV — a song about friendship and belonging, playing ironically as Rachel faces the loss of her romantic hope.
jokes.explanation: A clever meta-television gag — using the Cheers theme as ironic commentary on the Friends characters' emotional state. It's also a mild piece of NBC in-house self-referencing (both shows, same network). The juxtaposition of a comforting theme and emotional desolation is well-chosen. Gets rewatch bonus for the meta-layer.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's not over until someone says 'I do.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I do.

jokes.text: Monica describing the ruined wedding venue with optimism: 'Imagine a lot more lights, okay, and fewer bricks and flowers and candles...'
jokes.setup: Monica has brought Ross and Emily to what appears to be a bombed-out or demolished space to propose it as a wedding venue.
jokes.punchline: Monica's pitch requires imagining away most of the existing structure ('fewer bricks') — it's essentially asking them to imagine a completely different place.
jokes.explanation: Monica's optimistic hustle is funny — particularly 'fewer bricks' as a thing you have to imagine away from a wedding venue. It's not a sharp joke but it's functionally amusing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Wait, you can't leave! I'm pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, that's wonderful, but I have to go.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I'm carrying a litter. How many babies are you carrying?

jokes.text: Chandler, watching the romantic moment between Ross and Emily: 'Aw. I don't even have a date.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Emily share a loving moment about getting married in the rain; it's genuinely sweet.
jokes.punchline: Chandler undercuts his own emotional response — his 'aw' gives way immediately to self-pity about not having a date.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler: capable of genuine sweetness, immediately retreating to self-deprecating anxiety. The joke is in the speed of the pivot — 'aw' to 'I don't even have a date' in one breath. Very much the character's established lonely-man reflex.

dialogue.speaker: British Housekeeper
dialogue.line: When one answers the telephone, one should say 'Hello, this is the residence of...' not simply 'Yo, what's up?'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I'm just trying to be efficient. Why waste time with all that fancy stuff when you could just get straight to the point?

dialogue.speaker: British Housekeeper
dialogue.line: Because, miss, it is a matter of decorum and respect. One does not simply shout greetings into the receiver like some sort of... barbarian.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. Next time someone calls, I'll be all proper and British about it.

dialogue.speaker: British Housekeeper
dialogue.line: Thank you. Now, shall I prepare your afternoon tea?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Can you make it a Snapple?

jokes.text: He deserves to have all of the information. Then he can make an informed decision.
jokes.setup: Rachel has decided to fly to London to tell Ross she loves him, the day before his wedding.
jokes.punchline: She frames this act of romantic chaos as a rational, civic-minded information-delivery service — as if Ross is a consumer making a purchase decision rather than a groom.
jokes.explanation: Rachel rationalizing a deeply irrational romantic impulse in corporate-speak is very funny and character-specific. 'An informed decision' applied to a marriage proposal is an absurd framing that the character sincerely believes. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? I've had it with you! You think you're so fancy with your little accent and your perfect tea service. Well let me tell you something — if you don't shape up, I'm gonna take you to Chumpton-on-Thames and leave you there!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And Chumpton-on-Thames is NOT a nice place!

jokes.text: Phoebe to Rachel about why she's going to London: 'That's not why you're going. You're going because you hope he'll say: Yeah, I love you too, Rach. Forget about that British chippie.'
jokes.setup: Rachel insists she's going to London to give Ross 'all the information' so he can make an informed choice.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe cuts through Rachel's self-deception with brutal accuracy — and 'British chippie' as her term for Emily is a funny, specific phrase.
jokes.explanation: The 'British chippie' phrase is the best element here — Phoebe using British slang authentically in a funny way. The scene is also a good demonstration of Phoebe's often-underappreciated emotional insight presented through comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: She hung up on me! ...She must be on the other line with a rich guy.

jokes.text: Phoebe, unable to chase Rachel to stop her from going to London, shouts 'I do! I do! I do!' after her — a mock-wedding protest at Rachel going to ruin a wedding.
jokes.setup: Rachel rushes out to go to London despite Phoebe's pleas; Phoebe can't physically stop her.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe shouts 'I do!' — the wedding vow phrase — in a panic, as if her saying it will prevent Rachel from ruining the actual 'I dos' in London. It's simultaneously absurd and emotionally apt.
jokes.explanation: A clever bit of wordplay-meets-physical-comedy. The 'I do' repeated three times works on multiple levels: it's Phoebe's frantic non-verbal protest, it references the wedding vows about to be disrupted, and it's funny because she's shouting wedding words at someone going to disrupt a wedding. Phoebe being unable to give chase due to pregnancy makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Jack Geller
dialogue.line: In London, they call it a 'lift', not an elevator.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, Dad, I know. I lived there.

jokes.text: Phoebe, after her outburst: 'Yeah, like I can really chase you. I'm carrying a litter.'
jokes.setup: Rachel has already left; Phoebe's dramatic 'I do' outburst has achieved nothing.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe deflates immediately, acknowledging the obvious — she's very pregnant and couldn't chase anyone. 'I'm carrying a litter' is her self-deprecating assessment of her mobility.
jokes.explanation: 'I'm carrying a litter' is a genuinely funny self-description — using the word for animal multiple births to describe her triplet pregnancy. It's self-aware, absurd, and delivered at the perfect deflation moment. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Steven Waltham
dialogue.line: You're so self-involved.

dialogue.speaker: Andrea Waltham
dialogue.line: What? Who are the Gellers?

tmdb_overview:
The gang heads over to London for Ross and Emily's wedding. Joey can't contain his excitement about London which annoys Chandler to no end and results in two of them arguing. While the guys are touring the city, Monica, together with Ross and Emily, visit the chapel where the wedding ceremony is supposed to take place only to find out that it's being torn down prematurely.

Phoebe tries to warn the gang that Rachel is coming to London to tell Ross that she still loves him. After the initial excitement about visiting England dissipates, Joey begins to feel homesick, however, one of the bridesmaids helps him to forget about it. Meanwhile, Ross and Emily's parents get into an argument over the bill for the wedding.
insight: Season finale trades comedy for melodrama; 90 jokes diluted across romantic tension.
